<reason>Both sides were sharp and stayed on the motion, but B held the cleaner spine: a shrink is a price rise, disclosure restores a signal that unit pricing structurally cannot carry (it is cross-sectional, not intertemporal), and the implementation cost is near-zero because successor mapping already exists commercially. A's two best cards were the noise/undifferentiation point and the substitution-to-quality-degradation point. The noise point stayed partly live and was A's most memorable framing ("a warning on everything is a warning on nothing"), but B's reply — that widespread flags reveal the scale of what is currently hidden, and that the flag's function is to break the repeat-purchase habit loop and enable trade-down, not only to rank fourteen boxes — kept it from being decisive. On substitution, B's revealed-preference challenge (if quality degradation were free and unauditable, why do firms overwhelmingly choose the mould retool?) forced A to concede that shrinking is the cheapest tactic, which converts A's objection into B's own "raising the price of deceiving" logic; A's "near-tie tips" reply was plausible but speculative. Decisively, B answered A's expiry pressure squarely and memorably — an honest sticker rise is visible for one day, a flag for a year, so twelve months of being told beats zero days — and A never really rebutted that, only restated the objection. B also landed the attention turn: A cannot claim the shopper skips the shelf-edge annotation while proposing a bigger unit price as the remedy, since A had already asserted nobody consults the unit price. A's closing weighing was well-built and the debate stayed competitive, but B answered the harder pressure more directly and left fewer holes.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's answer to A's expiry question (A1 in Rebuttal 2, sharpened in closing): reframing "your flag lapses in twelve months" as "an honest price rise is visible for a single day, so twelve months of disclosure versus zero days is not an argument for concealment." A never overcame it and merely restated the objection in closing. B's paired attention contradiction — that A's own bigger-unit-price remedy dies first if attention is as scarce as A claims — was the second most damaging hit.</best_rebuttal>
